milestones.name: Touchdown
milestones.summary: The rover has landed on the de Gerlache crater rim and deployed from the lander.
milestones.howTo: Land on the Moon for the first time.
milestones.fact: The Soviet Luna 9 probe made the first soft landing on the Moon on February 3, 1966.
milestones.source: ESA, 3 February: Luna 9 (esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/3_February); NASA Science APOD text (science.nasa.gov/?p=1253718)

milestones.name: Odometer
milestones.summary: Total distance driven: {meters} m.
milestones.howTo: Drive {distances} in one mission.
milestones.fact: Apollo 17's Lunar Roving Vehicle covered about 36 km across three drives in December 1972.
milestones.source: NASA NSSDCA, Lunar Roving Vehicle (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/lunar/apollo_lrv.html): 35.9 km

milestones.name: Mapper
milestones.summary: The rover has surveyed {share}% of the map.
milestones.howTo: Explore {share}% of the map in one mission.
milestones.fact: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, launched in June 2009, maps the Moon; its laser altimeter, LOLA, measures the elevations used for polar terrain maps.
milestones.source: NASA Science, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (science.nasa.gov/mission/lro)

milestones.name: Crater descent
milestones.summary: The rover descended de Gerlache's inner wall, more than 120 m below the landing point, and climbed back out.
milestones.howTo: Drive down de Gerlache's inner wall, more than {depth} m below the landing point, and back out.
milestones.fact: With no wind or rain, lunar craters wear down only through small impacts, so they degrade over billions of years.
milestones.source: Fassett & Thomson (2014), Crater degradation on the lunar maria, JGR Planets, doi:10.1002/2014JE004698

milestones.name: Boulder field
milestones.summary: The rover crossed a boulder field on the rim of a fresh crater.
milestones.howTo: Drive across a rocky area, out the other side.
milestones.fact: Lunar boulders mostly come from impact ejecta, and the largest around young craters reach tens of meters across.
milestones.source: Pajola et al. (2019), boulder size-frequency distribution at Linné crater from LROC images (arxiv.org/abs/1812.00590)

milestones.name: Into the dark
milestones.summary: The rover entered the permanently shadowed crater and returned to sunlight.
milestones.howTo: Drive into the permanently shadowed crater and come back out.
milestones.fact: NASA's LRO Diviner instrument found that permanently shadowed regions near the lunar poles can get as cold as -414 °F (about -248 °C, or 25 K).
milestones.source: NASA SVS 11230, Diviner temperatures of the lunar poles (svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11230): shadowed regions as cold as -414 °F

milestones.name: Flare survivor
milestones.summary: A solar flare struck while the rover was protected. No damage was recorded.
milestones.howTo: Get through a solar flare without damage.
milestones.fact: With almost no atmosphere or global magnetic field, the lunar surface is fully exposed to solar energetic particle events.
milestones.source: NASA Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, Working on the Moon: Radiation (nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/alsj/WOTM/WOTM-Radiation.html)

milestones.name: Clean run
milestones.summary: The rover completed the mission without damage. The moonquake does not count: nothing can prevent it.
milestones.howTo: Finish all {days} days without damage (the moonquake does not count).
milestones.fact: ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 lander and Pragyan rover had a planned mission life of one lunar day, about 14 Earth days.
milestones.source: ISRO, Chandrayaan-3 details (isro.gov.in/Chandrayaan3_Details.html)

milestones.name: Crater layers
milestones.summary: The camera imaged the inner wall of the crater, where layers of rock can be exposed.
milestones.howTo: Photograph de Gerlache's inner wall from the wall descent point.
milestones.fact: Images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera show stacked layers of rock exposed in the walls of some lunar craters, such as Galilaei.
milestones.source: NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University, LROC featured image "Galilaei's Layered Wall", 4 January 2012 (lroc.im-ldi.com/images/457; NAC M160363453LE)

milestones.name: Regolith sample
milestones.summary: The drill collected a sample of lunar regolith, away from the ground the lander disturbed.
milestones.howTo: Drill a sample at least {minDistance} m from the lander. Up to {sites} sites, each {sampleSpacing} m from the others.
milestones.fact: The six Apollo landings brought back about 382 kg of lunar rock, core samples, pebbles, sand and dust.
milestones.source: NASA Astromaterials Curation, Lunar samples (curator.jsc.nasa.gov/lunar/)

milestones.name: Water ice
milestones.summary: The drill found water ice in the regolith inside the permanently shadowed crater.
milestones.howTo: Find the hidden ice inside the permanently shadowed crater and drill it.
milestones.fact: NASA's LCROSS probe struck Cabeus crater on October 9, 2009; the impact plume indicated about 5.6% water by mass in the regolith.
milestones.source: Colaprete et al. (2010), Detection of water in the LCROSS ejecta plume, Science 330:463, doi:10.1126/science.1186986 (5.6 ± 2.9%)

milestones.name: Earth on the horizon
milestones.summary: The camera photographed a sunlit Earth above the lunar horizon.
milestones.howTo: Photograph a sunlit Earth above the horizon, at least {earthMinDistance} m from the lander.
milestones.fact: From the lunar south pole Earth sits near the horizon, drifting a few degrees above and below it as the Moon librates.
milestones.source: Gorkavyi et al. (2023), Atmos. Meas. Tech. 16:1527, doi:10.5194/amt-16-1527-2023; NASA SVS 4944

milestones.name: Rim panorama
milestones.summary: The camera photographed the view from the de Gerlache crater rim.
milestones.howTo: Photograph the view from a rim viewpoint.
milestones.fact: De Gerlache Rim 2 is one of nine candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole that NASA named for Artemis III in October 2024.
milestones.source: NASA release 24-136, Oct 28, 2024 (nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-provides-update-on-artemis-iii-moon-landing-regions/)

milestones.name: Cold trap survey
milestones.summary: The neutron spectrometer measured hydrogen along a drive past a cold trap.
milestones.howTo: Switch the neutron spectrometer on and drive {meters} m that passes near or through a cold trap. Once for each cold trap, up to {sites}.
milestones.fact: In 1998 Lunar Prospector's neutron spectrometer found extra hydrogen near both lunar poles, and small cold traps that may hold ice turn out to be common there.
milestones.source: Feldman et al. (1998), Science 281:1496, doi:10.1126/science.281.5382.1496 (hydrogen, not proven water); Hayne, Aharonson & Schorghofer (2021), Nature Astronomy 5:169, doi:10.1038/s41550-020-1198-9

milestones.name: Hidden hydrogen
milestones.summary: The neutron spectrometer found hydrogen-rich ground outside the cold traps.
milestones.howTo: Somewhere near the lander the neutron spectrometer reads higher than in any cold trap. Find that ground and drive through it with the spectrometer on.
milestones.fact: LRO's LEND instrument reported hydrogen-rich areas near the south pole that do not match the coldest, never-sunlit ground; scientists still debate how strong that signal is. This spot is placed by design, inspired by that finding.
milestones.source: Mitrofanov et al. (2010), Science 330:483, doi:10.1126/science.1185696. Placed by design (Moon sites and milestones plan)

milestones.name: Ice deposit located
milestones.summary: The neutron spectrometer located a strong hydrogen signal: buried ice is close.
milestones.howTo: With the neutron spectrometer on, drive inside the permanently shadowed crater where its meter reads at least {percent}%.
milestones.fact: NASA's VIPER rover is designed to find hydrogen in the top meter of soil with its neutron spectrometer while it drives. VIPER has not flown yet: in 2025 NASA picked Blue Origin to carry it to the Moon.
milestones.source: NASA Science, VIPER rover and instruments (science.nasa.gov/mission/viper/rover-and-instruments); depth from NASA presentations; NASA release, September 2025 (Blue Origin task order to deliver VIPER)

milestones.name: Rock collection
milestones.summary: The X-ray spectrometer has now read several different rock types.
milestones.howTo: Read {rocks} different rock types with the X-ray spectrometer. Each site has its own rocks.
milestones.fact: Chandrayaan-3's X-ray spectrometer measured the soil near the lunar south pole as mostly ferroan anorthosite, with a magnesium-rich part.

milestones.name: Rare rock
milestones.summary: The X-ray spectrometer read magnesian norite, a rock found nowhere else on the map.
milestones.howTo: Find the one boulder of a rock found nowhere else and read it with the X-ray spectrometer. Once per campaign.
milestones.fact: The magnesium-rich part of the south polar soil may come from deeper rock, and LRO images show many boulders that rolled down crater walls. This boulder is placed by design, inspired by those findings.
milestones.source: Vadawale et al. (2024), Nature 633, 327-331, doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07870-7; Bickel et al. (2020), Nature Communications 11:2862, doi:10.1038/s41467-020-16653-3. Placed by design (Moon sites and milestones plan)

milestones.name: Boulder track
milestones.summary: The camera photographed a boulder that rolled down a crater wall, and the track it left.
milestones.howTo: Photograph the rolled boulder, in frame, from within {range} m.
milestones.fact: Scientists have mapped more than 136,000 boulders that rolled down slopes in Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images; most were set off by impacts.
milestones.source: Bickel et al. (2020), Nature Communications 11:2862, doi:10.1038/s41467-020-16653-3 (136,610 events)

milestones.name: Documented sample
milestones.summary: The camera photographed a boulder the X-ray spectrometer has read, recording where it lies.
milestones.howTo: Photograph a boulder the X-ray spectrometer has read this mission, in frame, from within {range} m.
milestones.fact: Apollo crews usually photographed rocks where they lay before collecting them, so geologists knew where each sample came from.
milestones.source: USGS Apollo 14 and 17 sample reports; NASA TR R-353 (Apollo 12)

milestones.name: Fresh ejecta sample
milestones.summary: The drill sampled fresh material thrown out by a young crater.
milestones.howTo: Drill a sample near a young crater or a rocky area, inside its ring of thrown-out rock, at least {minDistance} m from the lander.
milestones.fact: Material from fresh craters has had little time to be weathered by space, so it looks brighter than older ground.

milestones.name: Moonquake record
milestones.summary: The seismometer station recorded the moonquake.
milestones.howTo: Set the seismometer station down more than {minDistance} m from the lander, before the moonquake comes, so it records it.
milestones.fact: The Apollo seismometers recorded moonquakes for years; one of the strongest shallow moonquakes they recorded may have come from a fault near de Gerlache crater.
milestones.source: Watters et al. (2024), Planetary Science Journal 5:22, doi:10.3847/PSJ/ad1332

milestones.name: Clean seismogram
milestones.summary: The seismometer station's record of the moonquake is clean.
milestones.howTo: The seismometer station's moonquake record comes out clean.
milestones.fact: Apollo 17's seismometers recorded many small thermal moonquakes, set off as the ground warmed and cooled between lunar day and night.
milestones.source: Civilini, Weber & Husker (2023), JGR Planets, doi:10.1029/2022JE007704

milestones.name: Laser ranging site
milestones.summary: The laser retroreflector is on the ground, facing Earth.
milestones.howTo: Set the laser retroreflector down where Earth is in view, more than {minDistance} m from the lander.
milestones.fact: The reflectors Apollo crews left are still ranged with lasers from Earth, and in December 2023 NASA's LRO ranged the small reflector on India's Vikram lander.
milestones.source: Murphy et al. (2010), Icarus 208:31, doi:10.1016/j.icarus.2010.02.015; NASA release, January 2024 (LRO ranged the Vikram lander's reflector on December 12, 2023)

milestones.name: Science station
milestones.summary: The seismometer station and the laser retroreflector stand together: a science station on the Moon.
milestones.howTo: Set the seismometer station and the laser retroreflector down within {withinM} m of each other, more than {minDistance} m from the lander, with Earth in view. Once per campaign.
milestones.fact: Apollo 11 left a seismometer and a laser reflector side by side: the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package.
milestones.source: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, Apollo 11 EASEP crew handbook
